specPoints.text: understand the meaning of the terms: dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous, phenotype, and genotype

primer.text: Six words carry the whole of inheritance vocabulary, and exam questions fail on them more often than on the genetics itself. This note defines phenotype, genotype, dominant, recessive, homozygous and heterozygous, wires them to the PTC tasting example, and ends with the summary table to revise from.

lessons.title: The Six Vocabulary Anchors
lessons.opening: Six words carry the whole of inheritance vocabulary: phenotype names what you observe, genotype names the allele pair behind it, dominance lets one allele act alone, recessiveness demands two copies, and homozygous versus heterozygous describe whether the pair matches or mixes.
keyPoints: The phenotype is the set of observable characteristics of an organism.
The genotype is the allele pair an organism carries for a gene.
A dominant allele shows its characteristic with a single copy.
A recessive allele only shows when no dominant allele is present.
Homozygous means two identical alleles; heterozygous means two different ones.
Capital letters stand for dominant alleles and lowercase for recessive ones.

low.restatement: Genotype is the allele pair you carry; phenotype is the trait everyone can see.
low.analogy: Genotype is the handwritten order form; phenotype is the delivered parcel.
low.examPointer: Keep the PTC letters handy: T dominant, t recessive.

medium.restatement: Dominance decides which allele speaks in a mixed pair, and case convention encodes it on paper.
medium.analogy: A duet where the dominant voice sings over the recessive one, unless the recessive performs solo.
medium.examPointer: Watch the command words: define, then apply to fresh letters the examiner supplies.

check.stem: Which term names the observable characteristics of an organism?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Genotype is the allele pair, not the observable trait.
The genome gathers all the DNA, a different scale entirely.
Chromosomes carry genes; they are not the trait word.

check.stem: An individual carries two different alleles of a gene. What is the genotype called?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Homozygous requires the two alleles to match.
That term is not part of the taught vocabulary.
Recessive describes an allele's expression, not a mixed pair.

check.stem: When does a recessive characteristic appear in the phenotype?

options.text: Only when both alleles of the pair are recessive
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
A single recessive copy is masked by its dominant partner.
Dominant pairs hide it completely.
The homozygous recessive pair expresses it.

check.stem: In letter notation, how are dominant and recessive alleles written?

options.text: Dominant as a capital, recessive as the lowercase form
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Case is precisely what separates the two.
The dominant needs its capital.
The same letter is used, differing only in case.

check.stem: For PTC tasting, which genotypes produce the taster phenotype?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
The heterozygote also tastes, since T is dominant.
That pair lacks the dominant allele altogether.
tt produces the non-taster phenotype.

check.stem: Define genotype and phenotype in one sentence each.
check.modelAnswer: The genotype names the allele pair carried for a gene, and the phenotype names the observable characteristic that results.

check.stem: State the meanings of homozygous and heterozygous.
check.modelAnswer: Homozygous means the two alleles for a gene are identical, and heterozygous means they are different.

check.stem: Explain why a heterozygous individual usually shows the dominant characteristic.
check.modelAnswer: The dominant allele is expressed even as a single copy, so it masks the recessive partner in the heterozygous pair and decides the phenotype.

check.stem: A student records three plants with genotypes BB, Bb and bb for flower colour, where B is dominant. State the phenotype of each plant and the term for each genotype.
check.modelAnswer: BB is homozygous dominant, Bb is heterozygous, and bb is homozygous recessive; the first two plants show the dominant colour and the third shows the recessive colour.

lessons.title: The Summary Table and Fresh Traits
lessons.opening: The summary table compresses the vocabulary into one line per term, each with its definition and a concrete example, and the exam hint warns that fresh characteristics will replace PTC, so the relationships matter more than the memorised letters.
keyPoints: The table lists gene, allele, dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous, phenotype and genotype.
Each row pairs a definition with a concrete example.
Exam questions may hand you unfamiliar characteristics instead of PTC.
Apply the relationships between allele, genotype and phenotype to any fresh trait.

low.restatement: Revise the table row by row; each term needs its definition plus one example.
low.analogy: A packing list for inheritance questions: eight items, each with its purpose.
low.examPointer: When the examiner swaps in a new trait, rebuild the genotypes from the relationships.

medium.restatement: The rows chain together: alleles form genotypes, genotypes decide phenotypes, dominance sorts the outcomes.
medium.analogy: A flow: ingredients, mixture, finished dish.
medium.examPointer: Practise one unfamiliar trait end-to-end before the exam.

check.stem: In the summary table, which term is defined as a section of DNA?

options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
The allele row defines a version of a gene.
That row defines observable characteristics.
That row defines the allele combination.

check.stem: Which PTC genotypes from the table count as homozygous?

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Tt is the heterozygous row.
Tt carries two different alleles.
The mixed pair is not homozygous.

check.stem: The exam question hands you an unfamiliar characteristic instead of PTC tasting. What should you do?

options.text: Use the allele relationships, not the memorised PTC letters
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
The letters belong to the example, not the question.
The relationships transfer to any trait.
The examiner supplies the dominance information.

check.stem: Which table row pairs with the example Tt?

options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
That row shows TT.
That row shows tt.
The recessive example is the lowercase t alone.

check.stem: What single relationship runs through every row of the table?

options.text: Alleles form genotypes, and genotypes decide phenotypes
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
The causal arrow runs the other way.
The genotype mediates between them.
This table is about genetic relationships.

check.stem: Reproduce the table's definition of dominant.
check.modelAnswer: A dominant allele is expressed in the phenotype even when only one copy is present.

check.stem: Give the example listed for recessive in the table.
check.modelAnswer: The lowercase t allele of PTC tasting, which needs both copies for the non-taster phenotype.

check.stem: Explain why the same letter is used for a dominant allele and its recessive partner.
check.modelAnswer: The shared letter shows the two versions belong to one gene, while the case difference marks which one dominates, keeping the notation compact and unambiguous.

check.stem: A new trait called leaf curling is given to you with the information that allele C is dominant over allele c. Build the genotype for a heterozygous plant and state its phenotype.
check.modelAnswer: The heterozygous plant is Cc, and because C is dominant, the plant shows the curling characteristic.

glossary.definition: An allele expressed in the phenotype even when only one copy is present.
An allele expressed only when both copies of the pair are recessive.
Carrying two identical alleles for a gene.
Carrying two different alleles for a gene.
The observable characteristics of an organism.
